Instructions: Answer the following question about drug properties.
Context: Human intestinal absorption (HIA) measures the fraction of an orally administered drug absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract into the portal circulation. This is the first barrier to oral bioavailability — a drug must cross the intestinal epithelium before it encounters hepatic first-pass metabolism. Absorption occurs primarily via passive transcellular diffusion through the lipid bilayer of enterocytes, though carrier-mediated uptake (e.g., PEPT1 for peptide-like drugs, OATP for anionic compounds) and paracellular transport (for very small, hydrophilic molecules) also contribute.

Molecular features favoring high intestinal absorption: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-4) enables passive diffusion across the enterocyte membrane. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 120 Å²) is one of the strongest predictors — the desolvation cost of burying polar groups in the lipid bilayer is the primary barrier to transcellular transport. Limited hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 3-4) are more important than acceptors because donors form stronger interactions with water that must be broken during membrane partitioning. Molecular weight below 500 Da and moderate flexibility (rotatable bonds ≤ 10) favor absorption. Adequate aqueous solubility in GI fluids (pH 1-7.4) ensures the drug is dissolved and available for absorption.

Features associated with poor absorption: high TPSA (>140 Å²) is the strongest negative predictor. Zwitterionic or multiply charged species at intestinal pH have poor membrane permeability. Very polar, highly hydrophilic molecules (logP < -1) cannot partition into the lipid bilayer. Large, rigid molecules with MW > 600 Da have difficulty crossing the membrane. Compounds subject to active efflux by P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) or BCRP (ABCG2) at the apical enterocyte membrane experience reduced net absorption — Pgp substrates are pumped back into the lumen after partial absorption. Acid-labile compounds may degrade in gastric pH before reaching the absorptive surface of the small intestine.

(A) cannot be absorbed (B) can be absorbed

Context: Human intestinal absorption (HIA) measures the fraction of an orally administered drug absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract into the portal circulation. Absorption occurs primarily via passive transcellular diffusion through the lipid bilayer of enterocytes, though carrier-mediated uptake (e.g., PEPT1 for peptide-like drugs, OATP for anionic compounds) and paracellular transport (for very small, hydrophilic molecules) also contribute.

Molecular features favoring high intestinal absorption: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-4) enables passive diffusion across the enterocyte membrane. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 120 Å²) is one of the strongest predictors — the desolvation cost of burying polar groups in the lipid bilayer is the primary barrier to transcellular transport. Limited hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 3-4) are more important than acceptors because donors form stronger interactions with water that must be broken during membrane partitioning. Molecular weight below 500 Da and moderate flexibility (rotatable bonds ≤ 10) favor absorption. Adequate aqueous solubility in GI fluids (pH 1-7.4) ensures the drug is dissolved and available for absorption.

Features associated with poor absorption: high TPSA (>140 Å²) is the strongest negative predictor. Zwitterionic or multiply charged species at intestinal pH have poor membrane permeability. Very polar, highly hydrophilic molecules (logP < -1) cannot partition into the lipid bilayer. Large, rigid molecules with MW > 600 Da have difficulty crossing the membrane. Compounds subject to active efflux by P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) or BCRP (ABCG2) at the apical enterocyte membrane experience reduced net absorption — Pgp substrates are pumped back into the lumen after partial absorption. This is the first barrier to oral bioavailability — a drug must cross the intestinal epithelium before it encounters hepatic first-pass metabolism. Absorption occurs primarily via passive transcellular diffusion through the lipid bilayer of enterocytes, though carrier-mediated uptake (e.g., PEPT1 for peptide-like drugs, OATP for anionic compounds) and paracellular transport (for very small, hydrophilic molecules) also contribute.

Molecular features favoring high intestinal absorption: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-4) enables passive diffusion across the enterocyte membrane. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 120 Å²) is one of the strongest predictors — the desolvation cost of burying polar groups in the lipid bilayer is the primary barrier to transcellular transport. Limited hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 3-4) are more important than acceptors because donors form stronger interactions with water that must be broken during membrane partitioning. Molecular weight below 500 Da and moderate flexibility (rotatable bonds ≤ 10) favor absorption. Adequate aqueous solubility in GI fluids (pH 1-7.4) ensures the drug is dissolved and available for absorption.

Features associated with poor absorption: high TPSA (>140 Å²) is the strongest negative predictor. Zwitterionic or multiply charged species at intestinal pH have poor membrane permeability. Very polar, highly hydrophilic molecules (logP < -1) cannot partition into the lipid bilayer. Large, rigid molecules with MW > 600 Da have difficulty crossing the membrane. Compounds subject to active efflux by P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) or BCRP (ABCG2) at the apical enterocyte membrane experience reduced net absorption — Pgp substrates are pumped back into the lumen after partial absorption. Acid-labile compounds may degrade in gastric pH before reaching the absorptive surface of the small intestine.

This is the first barrier to oral bioavailability — a drug must cross the intestinal epithelium before it encounters hepatic first-pass metabolism. Absorption occurs primarily via passive transcellular diffusion through the lipid bilayer of enterocytes, though carrier-mediated uptake (e.g., PEPT1 for peptide-like drugs, OATP for anionic compounds) and paracellular transport (for very small, hydrophilic molecules) also contribute.

Molecular features favoring high intestinal absorption: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-4) enables passive diffusion across the enterocyte membrane. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 120 Å²) is one of the strongest predictors — the desolvation cost of burying polar groups in the lipid bilayer is the primary barrier to transcellular transport. Limited hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 3-4) are more important than acceptors because donors form stronger interactions with water that must be broken during membrane partitioning. Molecular weight below 500 Da and moderate flexibility (rotatable bonds ≤ 10) favor absorption. Adequate aqueous solubility in GI fluids (pH 1-7.4) ensures the drug is dissolved and available for absorption.

Features associated with poor absorption: high TPSA (>140 Å²) is the strongest negative predictor. Zwitterionic or multiply charged species at intestinal pH have poor membrane permeability. Very polar, highly hydrophilic molecules (logP < -1) cannot partition into the lipid bilayer. Large, rigid molecules with MW > 600 Da have difficulty crossing the membrane. Compounds subject to active efflux by P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) or BCRP (ABCG2) at the apical enterocyte membrane experience reduced net absorption — Pgp substrates are pumped back into the lumen after partial absorption. Acid-labile compounds may degrade in gastric pH before reaching the absorptive surface of the small intestine.

Instructions: Answer the following question about drug properties.
Context: Human intestinal absorption (HIA) measures the fraction of an orally administered drug absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract into the portal circulation. This is the first barrier to oral bioavailability — a drug must cross the intestinal epithelium before it encounters hepatic first-pass metabolism. Absorption occurs primarily via passive transcellular diffusion through the lipid bilayer of enterocytes, though carrier-mediated uptake (e.g., PEPT1 for peptide-like drugs, OATP for anionic compounds) and paracellular transport (for very small, hydrophilic molecules) also contribute.

Molecular features favoring high intestinal absorption: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-4) enables passive diffusion across the enterocyte membrane. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 120 Å²) is one of the strongest predictors — the desolvation cost of burying polar groups in the lipid bilayer is the primary barrier to transcellular transport. Limited hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 3-4) are more important than acceptors because donors form stronger interactions with water that must be broken during membrane partitioning. Molecular weight below 500 Da and moderate flexibility (rotatable bonds ≤ 10) favor absorption. Adequate aqueous solubility in GI fluids (pH 1-7.4) ensures the drug is dissolved and available for absorption.

Features associated with poor absorption: high TPSA (>140 Å²) is the strongest negative predictor. Zwitterionic or multiply charged species at intestinal pH have poor membrane permeability. Very polar, highly hydrophilic molecules (logP < -1) cannot partition into the lipid bilayer. Large, rigid molecules with MW > 600 Da have difficulty crossing the membrane. Compounds subject to active efflux by P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) or BCRP (ABCG2) at the apical enterocyte membrane experience reduced net absorption — Pgp substrates are pumped back into the lumen after partial absorption. Acid-labile compounds may degrade in gastric pH before reaching the absorptive surface of the small intestine.

This is the first barrier to oral bioavailability — a drug must cross the intestinal epithelium before it encounters hepatic first-pass metabolism. Absorption occurs primarily via passive transcellular diffusion through the lipid bilayer of enterocytes, though carrier-mediated uptake (e.g., PEPT1 for peptide-like drugs, OATP for anionic compounds) and paracellular transport (for very small, hydrophilic molecules) also contribute.

Molecular features favoring high intestinal absorption: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-4) enables passive diffusion across the enterocyte membrane. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 120 Å²) is one of the strongest predictors — the desolvation cost of burying polar groups in the lipid bilayer is the primary barrier to transcellular transport. Limited hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 3-4) are more important than acceptors because donors form stronger interactions with water that must be broken during membrane partitioning. Molecular weight below 500 Da and moderate flexibility (rotatable bonds ≤ 10) favor absorption. Adequate aqueous solubility in GI fluids (pH 1-7.4) ensures the drug is dissolved and available for absorption.

Features associated with poor absorption: high TPSA (>140 Å²) is the strongest negative predictor. Zwitterionic or multiply charged species at intestinal pH have poor membrane permeability. Very polar, highly hydrophilic molecules (logP < -1) cannot partition into the lipid bilayer. Large, rigid molecules with MW > 600 Da have difficulty crossing the membrane. Compounds subject to active efflux by P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) or BCRP (ABCG2) at the apical enterocyte membrane experience reduced net absorption — Pgp substrates are pumped back into the lumen after partial absorption. Acid-labile compounds may degrade in gastric pH before reaching the absorptive surface of the small intestine.

Context: Human intestinal absorption (HIA) measures the fraction of an orally administered drug absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract into the portal circulation. Absorption occurs primarily via passive transcellular diffusion through the lipid bilayer of enterocytes, though carrier-mediated uptake (e.g., PEPT1 for peptide-like drugs, OATP for anionic compounds) and paracellular transport (for very small, hydrophilic molecules) also contribute.

Molecular features favoring high intestinal absorption: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-4) enables passive diffusion across the enterocyte membrane. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 120 Å²) is one of the strongest predictors — the desolvation cost of burying polar groups in the lipid bilayer is the primary barrier to transcellular transport. Limited hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 3-4) are more important than acceptors because donors form stronger interactions with water that must be broken during membrane partitioning. Molecular weight below 500 Da and moderate flexibility (rotatable bonds ≤ 10) favor absorption. Adequate aqueous solubility in GI fluids (pH 1-7.4) ensures the drug is dissolved and available for absorption.

Features associated with poor absorption: high TPSA (>140 Å²) is the strongest negative predictor. Zwitterionic or multiply charged species at intestinal pH have poor membrane permeability. Very polar, highly hydrophilic molecules (logP < -1) cannot partition into the lipid bilayer. Large, rigid molecules with MW > 600 Da have difficulty crossing the membrane. Compounds subject to active efflux by P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) or BCRP (ABCG2) at the apical enterocyte membrane experience reduced net absorption — Pgp substrates are pumped back into the lumen after partial absorption. This is the first barrier to oral bioavailability — a drug must cross the intestinal epithelium before it encounters hepatic first-pass metabolism. Absorption occurs primarily via passive transcellular diffusion through the lipid bilayer of enterocytes, though carrier-mediated uptake (e.g., PEPT1 for peptide-like drugs, OATP for anionic compounds) and paracellular transport (for very small, hydrophilic molecules) also contribute.

Molecular features favoring high intestinal absorption: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-4) enables passive diffusion across the enterocyte membrane. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 120 Å²) is one of the strongest predictors — the desolvation cost of burying polar groups in the lipid bilayer is the primary barrier to transcellular transport. Limited hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 3-4) are more important than acceptors because donors form stronger interactions with water that must be broken during membrane partitioning. Molecular weight below 500 Da and moderate flexibility (rotatable bonds ≤ 10) favor absorption. Features associated with poor absorption: high TPSA (>140 Å²) is the strongest negative predictor. Zwitterionic or multiply charged species at intestinal pH have poor membrane permeability. Very polar, highly hydrophilic molecules (logP < -1) cannot partition into the lipid bilayer. Large, rigid molecules with MW > 600 Da have difficulty crossing the membrane. Compounds subject to active efflux by P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) or BCRP (ABCG2) at the apical enterocyte membrane experience reduced net absorption — Pgp substrates are pumped back into the lumen after partial absorption. Acid-labile compounds may degrade in gastric pH before reaching the absorptive surface of the small intestine.

Instructions: Answer the following question about drug properties.
Context: Human intestinal absorption (HIA) measures the fraction of an orally administered drug absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract into the portal circulation. This is the first barrier to oral bioavailability — a drug must cross the intestinal epithelium before it encounters hepatic first-pass metabolism. Absorption occurs primarily via passive transcellular diffusion through the lipid bilayer of enterocytes, though carrier-mediated uptake (e.g., PEPT1 for peptide-like drugs, OATP for anionic compounds) and paracellular transport (for very small, hydrophilic molecules) also contribute.

Molecular features favoring high intestinal absorption: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-4) enables passive diffusion across the enterocyte membrane. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 120 Å²) is one of the strongest predictors — the desolvation cost of burying polar groups in the lipid bilayer is the primary barrier to transcellular transport. Limited hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 3-4) are more important than acceptors because donors form stronger interactions with water that must be broken during membrane partitioning. Molecular weight below 500 Da and moderate flexibility (rotatable bonds ≤ 10) favor absorption. Adequate aqueous solubility in GI fluids (pH 1-7.4) ensures the drug is dissolved and available for absorption.

Features associated with poor absorption: high TPSA (>140 Å²) is the strongest negative predictor. Zwitterionic or multiply charged species at intestinal pH have poor membrane permeability. Very polar, highly hydrophilic molecules (logP < -1) cannot partition into the lipid bilayer. Large, rigid molecules with MW > 600 Da have difficulty crossing the membrane. Compounds subject to active efflux by P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) or BCRP (ABCG2) at the apical enterocyte membrane experience reduced net absorption — Pgp substrates are pumped back into the lumen after partial absorption. Acid-labile compounds may degrade in gastric pH before reaching the absorptive surface of the small intestine.

Compounds subject to active efflux by P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) or BCRP (ABCG2) at the apical enterocyte membrane experience reduced net absorption — Pgp substrates are pumped back into the lumen after partial absorption.
